chapter_title: Concerning Wisdom; it is far superior when on the Tongue than in the Heart of the Person.
chapter_note: This chapter contains no discernible cosmological-correspondential substrate. Teaching purity is 0.000 — the pipeline detected zero substrate vocabulary across all 17 paragraphs. The chapter is a self-contained Manichaean pedagogical dialogue using two natural SIMILES (child birth, fire in wood) to illustrate why wisdom is superior when proclaimed vs. hidden in the heart. Critically, the teaching uses simile ('like') rather than correspondential identity ('is'), distinguishing it from the substrate voice which directly identifies (e.g. 'The King of Wind IS eagle-face'). Both sides of every mapping remain in the natural/human domain (womb→open air, hidden fire→revealed fire) applied to epistemology (hidden wisdom→proclaimed wisdom) — no cosmic domains are mapped. The sole cosmic concept ('the Mind'/Nous in ¶16) is used illustratively, not systematically. The two-cycle dialogue structure (question→analogical answer→second question→extended analogies) appears to be an original Manichaean composition rather than a compilation wrapping pre-existing cosmic teaching.

paragraphs.temporal_note: Stereotyped dialogue opening: 'Once again, on one occasion, one of the disciples stood up before the apostle. He questioned him, saying: I entreat you, my master, that you might instruct me.' High dialogue_frame score (4.72). The disciple's question about wisdom is substantive but non-cosmological — it concerns epistemology (why wisdom shines more when proclaimed), not cosmic architecture. No cosmic domains, emanations, or systematic mappings.

Continues the disciple's question. Opens with frame marker 'That disciple speaks further before the apostle.' The question elaboration is philosophically substantive (reflecting on wisdom's enhancement through proclamation) but remains entirely in the epistemological/experiential domain — no cosmic vocabulary. All scores at 0.0.

Response frame: 'Then the apostle speaks to that disciple: Well do you ask!' High dialogue_frame score (4.65). The apostle's opening response restates the wisdom-proclamation theme but introduces no cosmic categories. The teaching that follows (wisdom superior in mouth than in heart) is pedagogical, not cosmological.

First analogy: child in womb → birth. Introduced by 'For like this matter, just so...' — explicit simile framing. The description is vivid and detailed (child turns in womb, emerges into 'the living open air that is more spacious than the first air he was in', fills eyes with light) but functions as illustration for the wisdom teaching, not as cosmic correspondence. Both sides of the analogy remain in natural/human domain. No cosmic vocabulary. Score: 0.0 across all layers.

Continuation of child analogy — comparing joy at conception vs. joy at birth. Purely illustrative. 'The love and joy over him shall be a hundred times greater' — numerical intensifier typical of pedagogical rhetoric. No cosmic vocabulary.

Continuation: hidden beauty (in womb) vs. visible beauty (at birth). 'His stature and his loveliness came before the eyes of his father and his mother and all his relatives.' The analogy extends to the social dimension (family seeing the child) which will later map to those who receive wisdom. Natural/social domain, no cosmic mapping.

Explicit simile application: 'Just as in this simile, the wisdom that is present in the heart of the person is LIKE the living child.' The word 'simile' (Coptic parabolē) marks this as conscious illustration, distinguishing it from the substrate's direct correspondential identification. The IS LIKE construction differs categorically from the substrate's X IS Y.

Application of the child analogy to wisdom: proclaimed wisdom advances, its glory doubles. 'Its enhancement and glory shall double from the time when the beauty and splendour of the saying will be displayed before the eyes of they who hear it.' Epistemological teaching, no cosmic vocabulary. All scores 0.0.

Second analogy: fire hidden in wood → fire revealed. 'the wisdom is like this... it is just like the blaze of fire that is hidden in wood.' Again, explicit LIKE framing. The fire-in-wood image is a classic ancient analogy (found across traditions), but here it functions as pedagogical simile within the dialogue, not as cosmic correspondence. Describes pieces of wood in a house, fire coming forth — natural domain only.

Application of fire analogy to wisdom: 'its light is hidden and its glory is hidden in the heart; but when the person will proclaim it, its glory shall be displayed before the eyes and the ears of a multitude.' Maps fire/light → wisdom/glory. Natural-to-epistemological simile, not cosmic mapping.

Second-cycle question opening: 'Once again, for a second time this disciple speaks to the apostle.' Formulaic transition to second Q&A cycle. The question — why do some rejoice in wisdom while others don't? — is substantive but non-cosmological. It sets up the extension of both analogies.

Pure response formula. Highest dialogue_frame score in chapter (16.0). 'Behold, the apostle speaks to him: I will persuade you and satisfy you about this belief, so that I teach you with clarity of vision.' Entirely formulaic transition with no teaching content.

Extension of child analogy: family rejoices but strangers grieve. 'These are not reckoned among his family. They do not rejoice over him, because he is not of their race.' Natural/social domain — explains differential reception through the kinship analogy. No cosmic vocabulary.

Application: 'When it is proclaimed by the mouth of the teacher, these who are akin to it shall receive it... but those who are strangers to it neither rejoice in it nor receive it.' The word 'teacher' triggers a low institutional score (3.85) but appears generic in context, not referring to a Manichaean institutional office. The kinship/stranger framework maps social categories, not cosmic domains.

Extension of fire analogy: 'whoever looks shall see the light... but whoever is blind does not see the fire.' The sight/blindness contrast parallels the kinship/stranger contrast of ¶13-14. Natural sensory domain, not cosmic mapping.

Application with the chapter's sole cosmic concept: 'The person, in whom is the Mind, of him is the wisdom... but the one who has no Mind in him is a stranger to it.' The Mind (Nous) is a cosmic entity in Manichaean cosmology, but here it functions illustratively — distinguishing wisdom-receivers from non-receivers — rather than as part of a systematic cosmic mapping. Not sufficient to establish substrate layer.

Classic dialogue closure formula: 'When that disciple heard these things, he rejoiced greatly. He was persuaded in his heart about what had been proclaimed to him. He made obeisance and sat down.' Stereotyped ending found across multiple Kephalaia chapters.
